events.text:
I found 63 superseded items corpus-wide; three have clean, readable quotes and confident matches (rerank margin > 2.2, no low_confidence flag). Here are three clear examples where the 18th-century Britannica fact is superseded by Wikipedia.

Direct answer: Three superseded facts — (1) Thomas Sydenham's death year (Britannica 1695; Wikipedia 1689), (2) the avoirdupois ounce as 1/15 of a pound (Britannica) versus 1/16 (Wikipedia), and (3) the Roman town Aternum identified as "now Alteris" (Britannica) versus the site of Pescara (Wikipedia).

Evidence

1. Thomas Sydenham death date
- Britannica [B:251:5]: "He died in 1695"
- Wikipedia [W:564669:1341167433]: "10 September 1624 – 29 December 1689"
- Inference: Britannica's 1695 death year is wrong; Wikipedia places his death in 1689, so the fact is superseded.

2. Avoirdupois ounce as a fraction of a pound
- Britannica [B:713:3]: "the fitteenth part of a pound avoirdupois" ("fitteenth" is OCR for "fifteenth", the long s read as f)
- Wikipedia [W:180279:1326550449]: "The avoirdupois ounce (exactly 28.349 523 125 g) is 1 ⁄ 16 avoirdupois pound"
- Inference: The 1/15-pound ounce is superseded; the modern avoirdupois ounce is 1/16 of a pound.

3. Location/modern name of Aternum
- Britannica [B:2171:9]: "ATERNUM, a town of Lucerna in Italy, now Alteris"
- Wikipedia [W:13770710:1352684512]: "Aternum was a Roman town, on the site of Pescara, in Italy."
- Inference: The identification "now Alteris" is superseded; Wikipedia places Aternum at Pescara.

Citation ids and match confidence were copied directly from the find_drift results; none of the three was flagged low_confidence.
